reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and colposcopy guidance on vulval premalignant disease
clinicalPearls: Usual-type VIN (vulval high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) is driven by high-risk human papillomavirus, expresses p16, and typically affects younger women, often with multifocal or multicentric disease involving cervix or anus

Differentiated VIN is HPV-independent, usually arises on a background of lichen sclerosus or lichen planus in older women, and carries a disproportionately high and rapid risk of progression to invasive squamous carcinoma
Symptoms are non-specific and include persistent itch, soreness, or a visible lesion, but a proportion are asymptomatic and found incidentally
Lesions are clinically variable, ranging from white, red, or pigmented plaques to raised or eroded areas, so appearance alone cannot exclude malignancy
Diagnosis rests on adequate biopsy, and any suspicious or non-healing vulval lesion should be sampled rather than treated empirically
Vulvoscopy after application of acetic acid, with directed biopsies, helps map the extent of disease and identify occult invasion

Management is individualised and may include local surgical excision, ablative treatment, or topical immune-modulating therapy for usual-type disease, whereas differentiated VIN generally warrants excision because of its cancer risk
Long-term surveillance is essential because recurrence and new lesions are common, particularly in immunosuppressed women and those with persistent HPV
reference.pathophysiology: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia describes dysplastic change confined to the vulval squamous epithelium above the basement membrane. Two distinct pathways are recognised. Usual-type disease follows persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, which through its oncoproteins disrupts cell-cycle control and produces the surrogate marker of diffuse p16 positivity; it tends to occur in younger women and is frequently multifocal. Differentiated VIN is unrelated to HPV and instead develops within chronically inflamed skin, classically lichen sclerosus, where cumulative genetic damage in the basal keratinocytes drives neoplasia; despite often subtle histology it progresses to invasive squamous carcinoma more readily and more quickly than the usual type.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic vulval dermatoses and candidal or contact dermatitis
additionalInvestigations: Vulval biopsy for histological confirmation and grading
Vulvoscopy with acetic acid to delineate lesion extent and guide directed biopsies
p16 and HPV testing to distinguish usual-type from differentiated disease
Colposcopic assessment of the cervix, vagina, and anus given multicentric potential
Assessment of the perianal region and mapping biopsies where multifocal disease is suspected
Screening for immunosuppression, including HIV testing where clinically appropriate
redFlags: Ulceration, induration, bleeding, or a nodular lesion suggesting occult invasion
Rapidly enlarging or non-healing lesion, particularly on a background of lichen sclerosus
Differentiated VIN histology, which mandates prompt excision because of high malignant potential
Recurrent or persistent disease in an immunosuppressed woman
New pigmented lesion raising concern for melanoma
reference.prognosis: Usual-type VIN may occasionally regress but frequently persists or recurs and can progress to invasive carcinoma, whereas differentiated VIN carries a substantially higher and faster risk of malignant transformation; with adequate treatment and lifelong surveillance most women avoid invasive cancer, though recurrence is common.
pitfalls: Treating a suspicious vulval lesion empirically without biopsy and missing invasive carcinoma
Overlooking differentiated VIN because its histological changes are subtle and the lesion may look like benign lichen sclerosus
Failing to examine the cervix, vagina, and anus in usual-type disease with multicentric potential
Discharging women prematurely when recurrence and metachronous lesions are common
Attributing persistent vulval itch to candidiasis or dermatitis and delaying diagnosis
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on vulval disease
National colposcopy and vulval premalignancy management guidance
management: Excise differentiated VIN and any lesion with suspected occult invasion by wide local excision with histological margin assessment
Use ablative treatment such as carbon dioxide laser for multifocal usual-type disease to preserve vulval anatomy and function
Offer topical imiquimod as a tissue-sparing option for usual-type, HPV-associated disease
Treat the underlying lichen sclerosus or lichen planus driving differentiated VIN with a potent topical corticosteroid
Advise smoking cessation and HPV vaccination, and optimise management of any immunosuppression
Screen for multicentric disease at the cervix, vagina and anus given field change
Maintain lifelong vulvoscopic surveillance with a low threshold to re-biopsy non-healing or changing lesions, coordinated through a specialist vulval clinic
